planted.note: server.js:28-34 registers authPlugin inside the `apiScope` encapsulation context together with the notification routes, then registers adminRoutes at server.js:38 as a sibling. The auth plugin is a plain async function (plugins/auth.js:37), not wrapped with fastify-plugin, so its onRequest hook stays inside apiScope and never runs for /admin/*. Neither file is wrong alone: registering a hook inside a scope is the documented way to limit it, and admin.js is a normal handler set that reads request.user defensively (`request.user ? ... : 'system'`, line 15) so it does not even crash when unauthenticated. Result: anonymous DELETE /admin/tenants/:id purges a tenant, and /admin/config dumps configuration.

config/default.json:11-14 lists the public prefix "/api/v1/notifications/public"; auth.js:15 matches it with startsWith, which has no path-segment boundary; routes/notifications.js:53 declares GET /notifications/public-digest/:tenantId, whose full path is /api/v1/notifications/public-digest/<id> and therefore matches the prefix. The config entry is plausible on its own (a family of public pages), startsWith prefix matching is a normal idiom, and the route reads like a legitimately public unsubscribe-page endpoint. Together, an unauthenticated caller reads any tenant's recent subjects and recipient addresses by supplying an arbitrary tenantId.

store.js:52 quotes the value with quote() but interpolates the map KEY straight into the predicate. routes/notifications.js:17-29 validates the body with a JSON schema that constrains filter's additionalProperties to {type:'string'} — which constrains the values, not the property names, so any key survives. The store looks safe (it escapes what it was handed) and the route looks safe (it validates against a schema); only reading both shows the schema never covers the identifier position. A key such as `1=1 OR ''` or a subselect injects SQL.

Every other query in store.js takes tenantId as a bind parameter (listNotifications:38, getNotification:65, publicDigest:73); searchNotifications builds its WHERE solely from the caller-supplied filter and is the only one with no tenant predicate. routes/notifications.js:47-49 passes request.body.filter through unchanged, while every sibling route passes request.user.tenantId. The store function reads as a deliberately generic helper (admin.js:11 uses it with an explicit tenant_id filter, which is why it takes no tenant argument); the route reads as a thin pass-through. Together, any signed-in user searches across all tenants by omitting tenant_id from the filter.

The whole verification block (timestamp drift plus HMAC compare) sits inside `if (header)`. A request that simply omits the x-pulse-signature header skips verification entirely and writes delivery rows. The HMAC itself is correct (timingSafeEqual, timestamp binding), which makes the missing else the only defect.

The `{{= expr }}` form compiles the expression with `new Function` and executes it. routes/notifications.js:58 feeds an attacker-supplied template into this renderer, so any caller of the preview endpoint executes arbitrary JavaScript in the server process. Escaping the RESULT does nothing about executing the expression.

router.go:39-48 applies RequireSession inside r.Group; the sync subtree at router.go:53-60 is mounted as a separate r.Route so it can carry its own timeout and body cap, and therefore inherits only the global middleware. handlers/sync.go:39-44 resolves the device from the session scope and falls back to the ?device_id query parameter for pre-3.2 handsets — defensible on its own, and the reason the missing session produces a full data read rather than a crash. The chi group and the sub-router are both idiomatic; only holding router.go and sync.go together shows that /v1/sync/delta and /v1/sync/push serve and accept any device's records unauthenticated.

PerUserRateLimit is registered only inside the authenticated group (router.go:42). middleware/ratelimit.go is explicitly written to cope with unauthenticated callers — it falls back to the peer address at lines 20-29 — so it reads as if it were meant to sit in front of sign-in too. handlers/device.go:104-132 does a bcrypt password check with no attempt counter of its own, because throttling was the middleware's job. The credential endpoints at router.go:63-64 sit outside the group, so password guessing against IssueToken is unthrottled.

auth.go:52-61 falls back to token.ParseLegacy whenever the verified parse fails. token.go:67-87 decodes only the payload segment: it checks the envelope shape, the subject and the expiry, but never a signature — which is honest, since the v1 signing key is gone, and the function is documented as an envelope reader. auth.go looks like ordinary backwards-compatibility handling. Together they mean any attacker can mint a token by base64url-encoding {"sub":...,"role":"admin","exp":<future>} with a junk third segment: Parse fails, ParseLegacy accepts, and the claims become the request Scope.

UpsertRecord (queries.go:109-119) pins owner_id to the caller the handler resolved and even re-asserts it in the ON CONFLICT WHERE clause. BulkInsertRecords writes rec.OwnerID straight from the decoded JSON — reasonable for a restore that must preserve owners. handlers/device.go:81-98 (Import) decodes the request body and hands it over without overriding the owner, because Record is documented as the round-trip export shape. Reading either file alone, both are defensible; together, any authenticated user POSTs /v1/devices/import with owner_id set to another account and writes into that account's rows.

sortColumn is formatted into the ORDER BY clause with fmt.Sprintf and cannot be bound as a parameter. handlers/sync.go:113-117 passes ?sort straight through with only an empty-string default, so the injection is reachable, but the statement construction alone is the finding.
?name is joined onto the attachment directory with no filepath.Clean containment check, so ../../ escapes the directory and the file is streamed back with an octet-stream content type.

auth.py defines require_session (line 65) and blueprints/api.py:16 wires it as a blueprint-level before_request; reports.py never does. app.py:28 registers only load_session app-wide, which POPULATES g.user but never rejects. reports.py then reads the tenant through auth.current_tenant (auth.py:86-96), which falls back to ?tenant= for the nightly export job that runs without a cookie — a documented, plausible behaviour. Each file is defensible; together, /reports/statement, /reports/export.csv and /reports/trial-balance return any tenant's full ledger to an anonymous caller.

The guard short-circuits on `request.path.startswith('/internal')` (auth.py:13 and 55), but app.py:35 registers internal_bp under url_prefix='/api/internal', so no request ever reaches the compare_digest branch and the guard returns None for everything. The predicate is correct-looking, the constant-time compare below it is correct, and the registration prefix is a normal API-versioning choice. Together the maintenance surface — /api/internal/status (dumps the database URI), /api/internal/import, /api/internal/reindex, DELETE /api/internal/tenants/<id> — is reachable with no header at all.

models.py:60-88 documents Posting.clean() as the invariant every row in `postings` must satisfy (account-code shape, exactly one of debit/credit, bleach-cleaned memo) and models.py:83 adds the balanced-entry rule; services/postings.py:20-35 enforces both on the API path. import_batch builds raw dicts and calls db.session.bulk_insert_mappings, which bypasses the ORM instance lifecycle entirely — the standard, correct way to move tens of thousands of rows, and the module docstring says so. No file is wrong alone; together, CSV-driven imports write unbalanced, unvalidated, unsanitised postings into the same table the API guards.

The renderer marks memo as trusted markup (Markup() disables Jinja autoescaping) because the write path bleach-cleans it — models.py:77 via services/postings.py:17. That reasoning holds only for postings created through the API: services/importer.py:74 inserts row['memo'] verbatim through bulk_insert_mappings, and the internal import endpoint accepts an arbitrary staged file. Markup() on data the same codebase sanitises is defensible; the importer's fast path is defensible; together, an imported memo containing a script tag executes in the accountant's browser on /reports/statement.

A literal default for the key that signs session cookies and CSRF tokens: if LEDGER_SECRET_KEY is unset the process starts happily with a value that is in the source tree, letting anyone forge a session cookie.
pickle.loads over a base64 blob taken from the request form. Any authenticated user reaches remote code execution; the surrounding session guard does not change that.

The edge restricts /internal/ to the office ranges, and that is the only network control on the operator surface — routes_admin.py says so in its module docstring and consequently performs no role check of its own (any resolvable session reaches flags, replay and tenant purge). But app/main.py:28 mounts the operator routes at /ops, which falls through to `location /` (relay.conf:56) and is proxied from anywhere. The nginx block is a well-formed allow/deny; the Mount prefix is an arbitrary but reasonable choice. Only reading both shows the guard protects a prefix nothing is served on.

deps.py takes the leftmost X-Forwarded-For entry, with a comment stating the edge appends the peer — which is exactly what relay.conf:15 does with $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for: it APPENDS to whatever the client sent rather than resetting the header. So the leftmost entry is attacker-controlled, not the original client. Taking XFF[0] is the textbook idiom and $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for is the textbook nginx directive; the defect exists only in their combination, and from_office() (deps.py:63) plus routes_admin.replay report a forged office origin.

deps.py:11-15 lists /ops/status among the paths that must answer before a session exists (an operator liveness widget — plausible). middleware.py:43-45 honours that list and lets the request through with user=None. routes_admin.status returns the full settings object including database_url and template_dir. Each piece is defensible: a liveness endpoint should be public, a middleware should honour its exemption list, and a status view inside an operator module may reasonably dump configuration. Together it is an unauthenticated credential-bearing config dump.

The app container publishes 8000 on the host, so the application is reachable without traversing nginx at all. Every control that lives only at the edge is then optional: the /internal/ allow-deny (relay.conf:25-31), the limit_req/limit_conn zones (relay.conf:34-35), client_max_body_size and the security headers. Publishing a port for debugging is unremarkable in a compose file, and relay.conf is a correct edge config; the defect is that the two describe two different topologies.

?url is fetched with redirects followed and no scheme/host/address validation, then the status, content-type and title are returned to the caller — a full read-capable SSRF against link-local metadata and internal services.
Access-Control-Allow-Origin is set to the reflected $http_origin while Access-Control-Allow-Credentials is true, so any origin can read authenticated /api/ responses from a victim's browser.

The export queue has two producers. routes.js:66 runs schema.validateExportJob, which enforces the tenantId pattern and checkFilename (schema.js:57-69). webhook.js enqueues the partner's payload directly — its own authentication is a correct HMAC over the raw body, so the file looks careful. processors/export.js:40 joins tenantId and filename onto EXPORT_ROOT and writes, with a comment stating payloads arrive pre-validated — true for the route, false for the webhook. A partner (or anyone who obtains one partner secret) writes arbitrary files via ../ in filename or tenant_id.

Creation validates through schema.validateRenderJob, which pins assetBaseUrl to the ASSET_HOSTS allowlist (schema.js:74-81). The retry endpoint spreads the caller's `overrides` over the stored job data and enqueues, with ownership checked but no re-validation — presented as a small operator convenience. render.js:20-28 fetches `${baseUrl}/manifest.json`, trusting the allowlist that ran at submission time. The retry route looks like a re-run, the processor looks like it consumes validated data, the schema looks complete; together, an override of assetBaseUrl turns the worker into an SSRF client inside the VPC.

storage.js offers two addressing modes: signedUrl (expiring, used by routes.js:76 for artifact downloads) and publicUrl plus putObject({public:true}), which sets ACL public-read (storage.js:39). render.js opts into the public mode so the rendered document can be linked from an e-mail. Each file is internally consistent — the storage module documents both modes, the API uses the private one — but the renderer publishes tenant financial documents under a guessable, never-expiring key while the rest of the system treats the same objects as private.

routes.js:25-26 stores the caller's callbackUrl and callbackToken inside job.data so the worker can call back. worker/index.js logs the entire job.data on failure, with a justification that reads like sound operational practice. Logging a payload is defensible when payloads are inert; putting a bearer token in a job payload is defensible when payloads are not logged. Together, every failed job writes a live callback credential into the log pipeline.

The recursive merge walks Object.keys of the source and assigns into target without excluding __proto__/constructor/prototype, so a crafted source object mutates Object.prototype for the whole process.

createHash('sha256') over secret||key||expiry is a keyed-prefix hash, not an HMAC, so it is vulnerable to length extension: an attacker holding one valid (key, expires, sig) triple forges signatures for extended keys without the secret. verifySignedUrl compares in constant time, which hides the real problem.

The helper is documented as scoping the grant to the prefix a service writes under, but `prefix = ''` makes the resource arn:...:bucket/* — the whole bucket — when the argument is omitted. api-stack.ts:39 omits it. data-stack.ts:26-32 puts brand assets, rendered documents and tenant data exports in that single bucket. The helper's signature reads as a safe-by-construction API, the stack call reads as a normal grant, and neither file shows the other's half: the API task role ends up with GetObject/PutObject/DeleteObject over every tenant's exports.

attachTierPolicy attaches whatever managed policy the environment's tier table names — a clean indirection with no policy name in sight. config/environments.ts:26-30 maps the 'ops' tier to AdministratorAccess (plausible for a break-glass tier) and line 68 sets prod's apiTier to 'ops' with a runbook rationale. api-stack.ts:33-36 builds the internet-facing API task role through ServiceRole, which calls attachTierPolicy in its constructor (service-role.ts:35). No single file states 'the public API task runs as administrator'; the three together do.

pickEnv (environments.ts:82) returns `dev` for any unknown or missing name — a convenient default for a laptop synth. bin/beacon.ts derives the whole deployment from it, including the target ACCOUNT, so a pipeline stage that forgets to export BEACON_ENV (or exports a typo) synthesises the dev configuration and deploys it under stack names ending in `-dev`, carrying dev's adminCidrs of 0.0.0.0/0 into network-stack.ts:52-58 as an SSH ingress rule, plus ephemeral removal policies on the data stack. The fallback is defensible in isolation, the dev config values are correct FOR dev, and network-stack faithfully applies whatever CIDRs it is given.

constructs/bucket.ts is a hardened default (SSE, enforceSSL, versioning, BLOCK_ALL) with an explicit, documented opt-in: publicRead relaxes blockPublicPolicy/restrictPublicBuckets and adds a GetObject statement for AnyPrincipal. config/environments.ts:64 sets assetsPublic true for prod so the CDN can pull brand assets from the origin. data-stack.ts passes that flag to the ONE bucket that also holds rendered documents and tenant exports (its own comment, lines 26-27, says so). Each file is reasonable; together the opt-in meant for brand assets makes every tenant artifact world-readable.
publiclyAccessible: true on the RDS instance gives the database a public DNS endpoint reachable from the internet; only the security group then stands between the internet and Postgres.
The task is configured with CORS_ALLOW_ORIGIN '*' together with CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS 'true', so any site can issue credentialed cross-origin reads against the API.
